📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia.
  • Industry observers note that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W.
  • Industry observers note that those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

Industry observers note that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

Industry observers note that those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

Recent findings suggest that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

Industry observers note that but most of this debate missed the point. No one—or at least very few people—would deny that we have seen ties between China and Russia grow in recent years. The use of the axis framing, however, and of language like “malice,” creates a narrative that does not necessarily exist in practice. It suggests that the only response to growing alignment between these states is adversarial, inhibits us from any real debate about the extent and scope of this coordination, and perhaps most importantly, suggests that this process of alignment is inevitable, rather than something that can be molded or changed. Such overly simplistic and Manichaean visions weaken, rather than strengthen, our ability to understand the world.

Recent findings suggest that none of this is latest. The “axis of evil” first emerged as a term in President George W. Bush’s 2002 State of the Union address, where he referred to Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as countries that endangered freedom around the world. Even at the time, the inclusion of the line in the speech was somewhat strange: It took place just a few months after the Sept. 11 attacks, and shortly after the United States had invaded Afghanistan, yet the three countries representing “evil” had nothing to do with either.

Industry observers note that but the overblown rhetoric helped to build support for Bush’s Freedom Agenda by reinforcing the idea that dictatorships around the world could endanger daily life in democracies. It attempted to tie the war on terror to the legacy of World War II through implicit comparison to Nazi Germany and imperial Japan. The speech had real-world consequences: It helped the Bush administration build the case for its war against Iraq and undermined the thawing of relations between the United States and Iran that had started shortly after 9/11.

According to recent reports, since that time, there have been repeated attempts to revive the axis concept to make a political or foreign-policy point. In just the last few years alone, there have been articles about the axis of authoritarians, the axis of upheaval, and the axis of aggressors. All these formulations offer authors the same opportunity: Pick a selection of nations and define them, not on their own terms, but on yours.

The axis of authoritarians, for example, relies on regime type to tie together its members, though the list of countries involved (Russia, Iran, North Korea, Belarus, and China) includes unreformed Soviet-style totalitarian regimes, kleptocratic dictatorships, and party-rule capitalism. This group includes one of the world’s richest states—and one of its poorest. The axis of upheaval, meanwhile, is defined by countries’ opposition to the United States, or by their shared commitment to “overturn[ing] the global order.” In truth, one could have an axis of almost anything; one is reminded of the old joke from around the time of Bush’s initial speech that suggested groupings including the “axis of just as evil” and the “axis of countries that aren’t the worst but certainly won’t be asked to host the Olympics.”.

Recent findings suggest that jokes aside, there is no denying that there are points of convergence and cooperation between the states referenced in these groupings. The reporting that accompanies the axis of malice story, for example, identifies a shared interest in the sanctions-busting “shadow” oil trade as a key area of cooperation among Russia, China, and Iran. Russia and China are cooperating on defense industrial issues, while Russia has built stronger ties with both Iran and North Korea due to its war in Ukraine and the search for cheap drones and easily replaceable domestic labor. There is a very clear case to be made that the bilateral relationships between many of these countries have grown stronger in recent years, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

Skeptics of the axis notion, however, would argue that many of these areas of cooperation were themselves driven by U.S. sanctions policy, not sought out by the states in question. There are clear tensions between Moscow and Beijing when it comes to North Korea, while China has been remarkably reticent in supporting either Russia’s war in Ukraine or Iran’s war with the United States. The evidence of growing bilateral ties between states is not matched by evidence of a common front among these states. Looked at holistically, many of their actions can just as easily by explained as states that find their interests—at least temporarily—pointing in the same direction.

Regardless of whether the skeptics or proponents of a more integrated partnership among these states are correct, this is an important debate. Indeed, it’s vitally important for U.S. policymakers to understand the scope and extent of cooperation between potentially adversarial states. The axis framing itself, however, is fundamentally unhelpful in moving these debates forward.

Industry observers note that for one thing, formulations like axis of upheaval and axis of malice are less descriptive than prescriptive: They always suggest the worst, and push policymakers toward the most hawkish options. Consider the description of growing China-Russia trade ties as “collusion.” Were the U.S. to engage in such trade with any of its allies, this would be considered perfectly normal behavior. Indeed, think tank papers are published every day in Washington talking of ways to increase resilience among the U.S. and its allies. The states under discussion here are often bad actors in world affairs, but adjectives like malice or upheaval suggest Manichaean actors implacably opposed to the United States with no nuance involved.

Industry observers note that the all-or-nothing nature of this framing also makes it more difficult to have discussions about the actual extent and scope of coordination between these states. By portraying them as a unified front—and by framing the debate as whether or not there is an axis—discussion often glosses over more interesting and potentially useful questions: Where specifically are these states cooperating? Are there limits to that cooperation? Are there issues on which they compete or where their interests diverge?

Perhaps most importantly, the notion of an axis of unfriendly states overlooks questions about how we got to this point—and whether this set of affairs must necessarily endure. At least some of the recent collaboration between these states has been shaped by U.S. policy choices, from sanctions and export controls on Russia and China, to the war in Iran and its effects in raising global oil prices. U.S. policymakers may still judge these policies to be worth the cost, yet it is fundamentally misleading to suggest that Russia, China, Iran, and others are pulling together purely to oppose the United States, when at least some of that coordination is a response to U.S. actions.

In a recent development, to put it another way: The idea of an axis of upheaval attempting to overturn global order strips the United States of its agency and replaces it with predestination. This is particularly vital when it comes to the policy responses. An axis of aggression cannot be reasoned with and it cannot be split apart, leaving little for the United States to do other than resist it. A more nuanced understanding of why these states cooperate—and where their common cause might fail—offers opportunities for the U.S. to undermine that alignment. If we understand the causes of adversaries’ alignment, we might be able to predict or even prevent it.

It’s easy to see why the language of the axis persists: It sells. But there’s a reason why such headlines should be relentlessly mocked. They deny us the ability to have a nuanced debate and reduce our policy options to an unsatisfying binary. For those who take U.S. foreign policy seriously, it’s past time to retire the axis of evil for good.

In a recent development, emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford.

Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's fresh executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Industry observers note that cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER.

Demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images).

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out newly introduced exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

In a recent development, "The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS.

President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP).

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit newly introduced exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

According to recent reports, cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory.".

It has been revealed that cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'.

It has been revealed that demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty).

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.".

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

President Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

“In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump said, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

Recent findings suggest that while voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he announced plans for another latest location next year.

“I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he mentioned of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

Trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

“I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” noted Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

“But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

Industry observers note that senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas said Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

In a recent development, “I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” noted Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

Trump on Monday showed how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private company, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

Industry observers note that in a Monday statement, Nvidia remarked its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Such unprecedented moves are a big reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week stated he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

According to recent reports, “Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” noted Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

Sources indicate that sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

“Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he said, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a latest system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

Recent findings suggest that north Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

“For the past two years, I have privately remarked there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the company and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain issues, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

According to recent reports, even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia remarked he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

Industry observers note that “I think the Nvidia matter has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine said. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

“If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump noted during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.

#134029. Tech Report: The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4651 w)

Tech Report: The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger.
  • According to recent reports, they are not entirely misguided in that belief.
  • The joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the Islamic Republic Can’t Make Peace.

It has been revealed that iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger. In 2026, the Islamic Republic survived a nationwide uprising and a devastating war with the United States and Israel that eliminated its leaders, decimated its military, and ravaged its economy. Yet rather than reconsider the principles and policies that have stoked nearly five decades of confrontation, isolation, and popular unrest, Tehran’s rulers drew the opposite conclusion: revolutionary ideology was not an albatross weighing the regime down, but a life preserver keeping it afloat.

According to recent reports, they are not entirely misguided in that belief. Since the 1979 revolution transformed Iran from a pro-American monarchy into an anti-American theocracy, the regime’s organizing principles have been the imposition of theocratic rule at home and resistance against Israel and the United States abroad. These policies have fueled recurring internal unrest and external conflicts that have impoverished, isolated, and destabilized Iran. Paradoxically, however, revolutionary regimes that survive such challenges often emerge more resilient, cohesive, and confident in their ideological convictions. The Islamic Republic, under the upcoming leadership of Mojtaba Khamenei, appears to be following the same pattern.

The joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime. It did, however, rally the regime around the revolution. Rather than embrace the possibility of a different political order, Tehran’s rulers closed ranks and extended the Khamenei era—literally, by anointing Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed his father, the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. “God’s grace is clear,” supporters chanted, “A young Khamenei is here!”.

At home, the war entrenched a revolutionary elite whose priority is resistance, not governance. That will only prolong the country’s crisis. The regime can suppress revolts but cannot address the conditions that produce them, leaving Iran trapped in a downward spiral of despotism, decline, and despair.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s attempt to resolve the Iranian challenge instead exacerbated it. The war, introduced in the midst of negotiations, has degraded Tehran’s military capabilities but hardened its revolutionary character, deepened its already profound mistrust of Washington, and taught its rulers a dangerous lesson: violence, not dialogue, secures concessions. Tehran has established fresh precedents for attacking its neighbors, disrupting global energy supplies, and asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Its leaders are determined to rebuild their military capabilities and avenge Khamenei’s death, while Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from restoring the capacity to threaten it. What Tehran may regard as necessary to rebuild its deterrence, Israel may regard as preparation for another war.

Industry observers note that washington can choose to end its war with Iran, but it cannot end the Islamic Republic’s confrontation with the United States. Israel cannot afford to ignore an adversary it regards as an existential threat. Gulf Arab states may have little say in whether Israel and Iran fight another war, but they could bear some of its greatest costs as their cities, energy infrastructure, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to Iranian retaliation. Tehran regards the Gulf’s economic and technological achievements not as examples to emulate, but as vulnerabilities to exploit and targets to threaten. For these reasons, the end of this war is likely to prove an intermission rather than a resolution.

The challenges the Islamic Republic poses to the Middle East, the United States, and the global economy can ultimately be resolved only with political change in Tehran. Yet getting through 2026 has simply reinforced the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary conviction that its survival is best ensured through continuity, not change. The country will remain suspended between war and peace abroad, and between prolonged decay and sudden upheaval at home. Iran is thus left in a paradox. Revolutionary ideology has led the country toward destruction. But abandoning revolutionary ideology could lead the regime toward collapse.

Like all ailing autocracies, the Islamic Republic has the potential to both gradually atrophy or abruptly implode. Russian Tsar Nicholas I first referred to the Ottoman Empire as “the sick man” of Europe in 1853; its end came seven decades later. George Kennan wrote in these pages in 1947 that the Soviet Union “bears within it the seeds of its own decay, and that the sprouting of these seeds is well advanced.” It took another 44 years for the Soviet Union to collapse.

The Islamic Republic of Iran has come to resemble the Leaning Tower of Pisa: seemingly on the verge of collapse but defying political gravity decade after decade. Despite its abundant natural resources and human capital, theocratic Iran has been a case study in squandered national potential. Its economy is trapped in recurring crises, its currency is ravaged by inflation, and generations of educated citizens seek their futures abroad. Nearly half a century after the revolution, Iran’s real GDP per capita remains nearly a quarter below its 1976 peak. That means that many Iranians are materially worse off than their parents and grandparents were before the revolution, an economic regression typically suffered only by failed states or societies ravaged by civil war.

In a recent development, while Iran’s economy has regressed, its society has progressed. Over the last five decades, its population has nearly tripled, and a predominantly rural and traditional society has become increasingly urban, educated, and socially liberal. Since the 2022–23 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, mandatory veiling—what Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once called the “flag” of the Islamic Revolution—appears increasingly unenforceable. Women now routinely walk down the streets of Tehran and other cities with their hair uncovered. The breaking of this taboo will embolden Iranians to break others. In short, Iran’s citizens look forward, Iran’s rulers look backward, and Iran’s economy spirals downward. It is a country whose people have moved beyond the revolution, but whose rulers refuse to leave it behind.

The historian Crane Brinton compared revolutions to fevers that eventually break, ushering in a period of moderation known as Thermidor. Yet many decades after the revolution, Iran’s rulers still refuse to lower the temperature. Iranian society has long sought a return to normalcy, but the regime fears that ending the revolution would mean ending its own rule. The growing gap between rulers and the ruled can be sustained only through continued brutality. The Islamic Republic’s aspiring Deng Xiaopings were sidelined for fear they might become the regime’s Mikhail Gorbachevs. Its Vaclav Havels have been imprisoned, exiled, or killed. Edmund Burke warned that “a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.” Yet the Islamic Republic’s rulers appear more willing to risk breaking the regime than to allow themselves to bend, and more willing to risk another calamitous war than to abandon the revolutionary principles that have sustained their power.

According to recent reports, revolutionary regimes are surprisingly resilient. As the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way write in Revolution and Dictatorship, such regimes tend to last nearly three times as long as their nonrevolutionary counterparts, despite being twice as likely to be involved in wars. Although their radicalism often triggers counterrevolution or external war, regimes that survive those early challenges commonly develop three pillars of durability: “a cohesive ruling elite,” “a highly developed and loyal coercive apparatus,” and “the destruction of rival organizations and alternative centers of power in society.”.

It has been revealed that the Islamic Republic has developed these three pillars because of, not in spite of, decades of internal opposition and near-constant hot and cold wars. The 444-day seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran beginning in 1979 and the eight-year war with Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, which began the following year, were foundational crises that brought international isolation and economic devastation to Iran but helped entrench Khomeini’s theocracy. Both were prolonged well beyond their initial objectives, in part because they served the regime’s internal consolidation: the hostage crisis marginalized moderates, while the exigencies of the war with Iraq smothered internal dissent and helped build the military-industrial system—namely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)—to entrench theocratic government. Just as the Long March forged the bonds and credentials of China’s revolutionary elite in the 1930s, the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s forged those of the Revolutionary Guard commanders who rule Iran today.

Whereas most states seek normalcy and the resolution of crises, crises in the Islamic Republic provided fertile soil for the revolution. As Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, the Islamic Republic’s first president, observed in 2003, after more than two decades in exile: “With the end of the war, crisis-making did not end. The mullahs’ regime, which was born of crisis-making, could not continue its life without making crises.” The Islamic Republic has made disequilibrium its equilibrium. Indeed, some within the regime privately believe that IRGC attacks on shipping during this year’s cease-fire, as well as the maximalist demands of Iranian negotiators, were meant to prolong the war and entrench the power of hard-liners, much as the Iran-Iraq War helped cement their position.

By attacking Iran weeks after the regime killed thousands of protesters, one of the bloodiest massacres in modern Iranian history, Trump provided Tehran with an external crisis to divert attention from its internal one. Imagine if the United States had attacked the Soviet Union in 1982, as its economy stagnated, its ideology languished, and its aging rulers struggled to preserve a discredited political order. Rather than hastening communism’s demise, such an attack might have revitalized its defenders, discredited its critics, and transformed a crisis of legitimacy into a struggle for national survival. Something similar seems to have happened in Iran. The war allowed Tehran’s rulers to portray their decades of hostility toward the United States not as the source of Iran’s predicament, but as vindication of their worldview. It is telling that while Israeli and U.S. forces have killed many of the regime’s top political and military leaders, no high-level officials have defected.

Industry observers note that no one in today’s Islamic Republic has the stature to push for reform or rapprochement with Washington; its many veto men, whose privileges depend on the status quo, have the power to block both. Profound change requires consensus. Inertia can be entrenched by a few.

Sources indicate that A great deal depends on the largely invisible Mojtaba Khamenei. It remains to be seen for how long the Islamic Republic’s political and military elite will defer to a supreme leader who has, for whatever reason, withdrawn from public view. Iranian political culture tends toward personality cults, and over much of the last century the country has largely been led by four strongmen: Reza Shah (1925 to 1941), Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi (1941 to 1979), Khomeini (1979 to 1989), and Ali Khamenei (1989 to 2026). Few major countries have experienced such extraordinary continuity of personal rule across radically different political systems. The present situation—an absent supreme leader hidden from public view, possibly for health reasons or out of fear of assassination, and competing centers of power within the security establishment—therefore looks like an unstable equilibrium.

According to recent reports, after Khomeini came to power, in 1979, outside observers commonly assumed Iran’s revolutionary fervor would fade and that the country’s upcoming leaders could be won over with the right mix of respect and economic inducements. “Khomeini will be somewhat of a saint when we get over the panic,” Andrew Young, a UN ambassador in the Carter administration, predicted in February 1979. “In two years, our relations with Iran will be on a pretty even keel.” But today, the regime still chants “Death to America.” Governments do not cling to policies that they believe endanger their survival. The enduring mistake has been to assume that Iran’s leaders cannot possibly mean what they repeatedly say.

Recent findings suggest that the Islamic Republic has always framed its conflict with the United States not merely as a geopolitical dispute but also as a moral and ideological struggle. Khomeini, who outlined his vision of Islamic government nearly a decade before the revolution and implemented it after seizing power, called the United States “the foremost enemy of Islam” in his last will and testament. His successor, Ali Khamenei, maintained remarkable ideological consistency over nearly four decades, repeatedly describing the rivalry as an “inherent conflict—an inherent incompatibility.” For both men, their publicly articulated convictions proved a far more reliable guide to the Islamic Republic’s conduct than the reassurances of its diplomats or the wishful interpretations of Western observers.

Sources indicate that khamenei’s son and successor Mojtaba—whose face and voice have not been seen or heard since he became supreme leader in March 2026—has echoed his father in his public pronouncements. “The criminal rulers of America and the illegitimate Zionist regime,” he said in one statement, “are not merely enemies of the Islamic Republic, Iran, or the vast front of Islamic resistance; they harbor enmity toward the entire Islamic ummah”—the Muslim community. After the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections in November, a post on Mojtaba Khamenei’s official English-language X account proclaimed that “the process of the US’s collapse has accelerated.” He further warned that neither American elections nor Iranian concessions would alter the “hegemonic system” of the United States and its hostility toward the Islamic Republic.

The elder Khamenei’s assassination at the start of the war continued the transformation of Iran from a country led by clerics into one dominated by current and former IRGC officers. Many observers assumed this shift from turbans to uniforms would move the regime’s focus from religious ideology to national interest. This has yet to happen. Although the regime has adopted more overtly nationalist rhetoric, it still subordinates the welfare and security of Iranians to the goals of the revolution. The motivations of security officials may be more financial than theological, but their interests have remained bound to the same revolutionary order.

In a recent development, siamak Namazi, an Iranian American who spent nearly eight years as a hostage of the IRGC in Tehran’s Evin prison, describes the Islamic Republic as a “competitive kleptocracy masquerading as a theocracy.” Many of the regime’s elite, he has observed, are driven less by religious dogma than by the spoils of power: preferential exchange rates, privileged loans, import licenses, and a cut of the smuggling trade. “The revolutionary Kool-Aid,” he mentioned, “is reserved for the ranks, because someone still has to believe enough to open fire on their own countrymen.” The true believers also have a great deal to lose. A January 2026 Bloomberg report alleged that Mojtaba Khamenei had used a middleman to build a financial empire in the West, including $138 million in British luxury real estate and Swiss bank accounts.

The IRGC has eclipsed the clergy in both political and economic power, with some estimates suggesting they control more than a third of Iran’s economy. Individual commanders have accumulated fortunes, often by enabling the business activities of their children, known as aghazadehs, or princelings. Yet rather than challenge the supreme leader, the senior command’s public statements suggest continued solidarity with the office. Mohsen Rezaei, a longtime IRGC commander with substantial family business interests who returned to serve as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, expressed his devotion to Mojtaba in a September 2026 interview with state television. “Let us preserve our unity,” he insisted. “Let us preserve our dignity. Let us march behind the leader of the revolution.”.

In a 26-page open letter to the American people published the same month, the IRGC declared that the war had “reinvigorated the Islamic Republic” and would ensure the regime’s survival for decades. Rather than question the ideology that had brought Iran to this precipice, the corps reaffirmed velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship, as an “embodiment of all godly virtues in the political sphere” that empowered Iran to stand firm against diabolical powers. Revolutionary and religious dogma were not the source of Iran’s predicament, they concluded, but rather the “main factors underpinning Iran’s victory.”.

Recent findings suggest that iran’s rulers are neither pragmatic nationalists guided by traditional state interests nor an apocalyptic death cult. They outsource the politics of martyrdom to regional militias while ruthlessly practicing the politics of survival at home. For the true believers, abandoning the revolution would mean betraying their convictions; for its profiteers, it would mean jeopardizing their power and privileges. When the regime’s survival is at stake, they may change their tactics, but they won’t change their worldview.

The war has left Tehran both weaker and much more aggressive. Before the war, the Islamic Republic resembled a zombie regime: its ideology, legitimacy, and its 86-year-old supreme leader all appeared to be fading. Since the outbreak of the war, it has come to resemble a gangster regime—one that practices extortion as statecraft—and is emboldened to attack its neighbors, the global economy, and the United States to extract concessions.

Tehran has been rewarded for its defiance by Trump. In his dramatic address launching the war in February 2026, Trump vowed to end Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions, destroy its missile capabilities, and neutralize its regional proxies. He encouraged Iranians to overthrow their “wicked” dictatorship. But the president soon changed his tune. Although Trump believed the war would be a swift “little excursion,” Iran’s attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and its over 6,700 missile and drone attacks on its Gulf neighbors compelled him to attempt one of the most striking reversals in modern American foreign policy.

In June, Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Tehran that gave away the store. He pledged to lift all sanctions as part of a final agreement, release frozen Iranian assets, permit Iranian oil exports, and work with regional partners on a $300 billion reconstruction package. The agreement also accepted an Iranian role in determining the future administration of the Strait of Hormuz, committed Washington to noninterference in Iran’s internal affairs, and made no mention of Iran’s missiles or regional proxies.

According to recent reports, in just four months, Trump had gone from pursuing the most hawkish Iran policy ever to offering the most generous diplomatic terms since the 1979 revolution. A policy of regime change became one of accommodation. Although the memorandum of understanding was short-lived—each side blames the other for abrogating it—the lesson Tehran learned was unmistakable: restraint projects weakness, whereas aggression is rewarded.

Sources indicate that “We seize concessions not through dialogue, but with missiles,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, a former IRGC commander, the current speaker of the parliament, and one of the regime’s most powerful figures. “The winner of any agreement,” he added, “is the one who is better prepared for war from the day after.” Tehran is already signaling that its chief postwar priority will not be to rebuild its decimated economy, but to restore—and expand—its ability to impose costs on its adversaries.

Sources indicate that the Strait of Hormuz offers the clearest example of this dynamic. What was once an Iranian threat has become, in Tehran’s eyes, an entitlement: the ability to regulate passage through one of the world’s most consequential energy chokepoints. For Iran, this constitutes both economic leverage and a potential deterrent against future attacks on itself and its regional proxies. For the rest of the world, it creates the prospect that Tehran can hold global energy markets hostage whenever it chooses.

In a recent development, before the war, the Iranian regime’s longtime ambitions to drive the United States from the Middle East and end Israel’s existence appeared fanciful. Today, the growing number of American politicians and commentators who have called for the United States to end its aid to Israel and wind down its regional military presence has emboldened Tehran to believe it is winning the ideological war. “POTUS clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on social media in November. He continued: “Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars. They had enough. So has our region.”.

The Islamic Republic’s newfound confidence is partly rooted in its ability to inflict enormous damage at comparatively little cost. Its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent decades and trillions of dollars transforming themselves into global hubs of energy, transportation, finance, and technology. And Iran can now threaten all of it with cheap Shahed drones against which the United States and its partners must field multimillion-dollar interceptors—a costly undertaking that Nick Carter, a retired British general and former chief of the British defense staff, likened to “Ferraris being thrown at Frisbees.” Building is costly and slow; destruction is fast and cheap. Rezaei has pledged to target undersea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across the Gulf in the event of renewed fighting.

In a recent development, the Islamic Republic’s theory of victory does not require defeating the United States militarily. It only requires persuading two audiences—the American public and Iran’s Gulf neighbors—that the U.S. military presence in the region and the partnership with Israel bring more harm than good. The attacks on American bases, Gulf data centers, and ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz are a message that the road to regional security must go through Iran, not the United States or Israel. “The nations and territories of the region will no longer serve as a shield for American bases,” Mojtaba Khamenei has declared.

It has been revealed that but this Iranian aggression is likely to produce the opposite of what it intends. Tehran’s threats against the Gulf only stoke the anxieties that sustain Washington’s military presence in the region. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle in which Gulf governments seek American protection against Iran, Tehran attempts to evict Washington from the region, and each upcoming round of conflict deepens the Gulf states’ dependence on the United States.

Sources indicate that iran’s confrontation with Israel poses a different, potentially more explosive danger. The regime’s hostility to Israel has survived the destruction of much of Tehran’s military infrastructure and its regional proxy network. Iranian leaders remain determined to rebuild their missile and drone arsenals, restore the capabilities of allies such as Hezbollah, and avenge the killing of Ali Khamenei. Yet Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from reconstituting the capabilities that threatened it before the war. Each side may therefore interpret the other’s attempts at deterrence as preparations for another attack.

As for Trump’s original justification for the war—to avert an Iranian nuclear bomb—his actions and words have persuaded a growing number of Iranian officials to openly advocate nuclear arms development. The president himself supplied Tehran’s talking points. “If they had a nuclear weapon,” Trump told a crowd of supporters six months into the war, “I’d be calling the supreme leader and I’d be saying: ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’—as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.”.

According to recent reports, since the 1979 revolution, Washington has tended to underestimate the Islamic Republic’s agency and overestimate its own ability to shape Iran’s future. Advocates of engagement often blame American hostility for Tehran’s intransigence, while advocates of confrontation have blamed American weakness. One side has overestimated the Islamic Republic’s flexibility; the other, its fragility. Both have been susceptible to what the former U.S. national security adviser H. R. McMaster has called “strategic narcissism”: the assumption that adversaries are primarily reacting to the United States rather than acting on their own interests, identities, and ambitions.

In a recent development, trump’s war exposed the limits of trying both to bomb Iran into submission and to bribe it into moderation. In the span of four months, Washington employed overwhelming military force to weaken or overthrow the Islamic Republic, then offered sweeping economic and diplomatic incentives to alter its behavior. Neither altered a revolutionary stance that has been remarkably consistent for decades. As Henry Kissinger wrote in 1957, “The distinguishing feature of a revolutionary power is not that it feels threatened . . . but that nothing can reassure it.”.

The seeds of the next war have already been planted. Regardless of what the United States chooses to do, the Islamic Republic’s renewed confidence, along with its resolve to rebuild its military might and retaliate for the death of its supreme leader, portends another showdown with Israel. Each side now views the other as an existential threat, and there is no direct channel of dialogue to prevent miscalculation and a potentially even more destructive war. For Washington, the implication is clear: The United States may seek to disengage from the Middle East, but it cannot insulate itself from the consequences of another war between Iran and Israel.

The Islamic Republic’s most consequential compromises came in 1988, when Khomeini reluctantly accepted a cease-fire ending the eight-year war with Iraq, and in 2015, when Iran agreed to stringent restrictions on its nuclear program. Although separated by nearly three decades, both decisions followed a similar logic. Faced with overwhelming pressure, international isolation, and a diplomatic off-ramp that does not require it to change its identity, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated a capacity to make concessions—but only in the service of living to fight another day.

In a 2013 speech foreshadowing Tehran’s nuclear compromise, Ali Khamenei described this approach as “heroic flexibility.” The supreme leader likened the regime to a wrestler who “reveals flexibility for technical reasons” but must never “forget who his opponent is and what he is doing.” Tactical flexibility, Khamenei insisted, must never come at the expense of Iran’s “revolutionary nature”: “The fact that the world has changed cannot give us an excuse to change our behavior, our ideals, and our goals.” Ali Khamenei had the legitimacy to push for heroic flexibility. The current regime is filled with men who will pursue escalation long before they ever call for compromise.

Today, the challenges posed by Iran are much greater than a decade ago. Washington must not only prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons but also deter it from attacking its neighbors, disrupting the global energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and waging AI-assisted cyberwarfare and influence operations against the United States and its partners. At the same time, Washington has fewer allies and less diplomatic leverage than it did in 2015, and the trust gap between the two governments may prove unbridgeable. The Iranian regime believes that global public opinion is on its side, not Trump’s.

Sources indicate that the 48-year history of U.S. policy toward the Islamic Republic shows that grand designs, whether for regime change or rapprochement, have failed. On two occasions, in 1988 and 2015, both sides reached narrow agreements that addressed Tehran’s conduct rather than its character. Lasting change, however, can come only from within Iran, when the pillars that sustain the Islamic Republic—a cohesive elite, a loyal coercive apparatus, and the absence of rival centers of power—crack. Rather than widening those cracks, Trump’s war may have narrowed them.

Industry observers note that iran’s rulers see the regime’s survival as proof of their own strength. Yet each crisis they weather leaves the country poorer, its people more estranged, and the regime more dependent on brutality to endure. Like Washington before it, Tehran now overestimates what force can achieve; its hubris may help produce the next war, just as the repression that quelled the last uprising will invariably fuel another. The revolutionary ideology that keeps the regime afloat will continue to weigh Iran down, leaving in place a leadership even more intent on resisting its adversaries, at home and abroad, than on governing its people. The regime may declare victory, but for the proud people of Iran—an ancient civilization and an energy superpower with a worthless currency, a shunned passport, and a leader in hiding—there is little reason to celebrate. What has not killed the Islamic Republic is slowly killing Iran.

KARIM SADJADPOUR is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory. First elected in 2018, Sánchez has established himself as Europe’s longest-serving social democratic leader. He has made Spain the best-performing economy in the European Union. His willingness to welcome immigrants, challenge U.S. President Donald Trump, and describe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a genocide have also turned him into an icon of the international left.

Sources indicate that but Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years. His government is mired in corruption scandals, his blanket amnesty for separatists involved in Catalonia’s illegal 2017 independence referendum has alienated many voters, and his plan to offer a pathway to citizenship to more than 500,000 undocumented immigrants has provoked a right-wing backlash. After more than eight years in office, he is also confronting considerable voter fatigue.

Now, a worsening housing crisis is threatening to become another political liability for Sánchez. Yet he also sees it as an opportunity: By making housing the defining issue of the election, he may be able to divert attention from his political vulnerabilities while mobilizing the left-wing voters he needs to remain in power.

Last month, Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for Nov. 29, roughly seven months ahead of schedule. His biggest electoral challenge is not defeating a surging right but mobilizing left-wing voters. If Spain’s center-right and far-right opposition parties take control of the government, it will likely be because many left-wing voters stay home. An estimated 1.4 million left-wing voters are expected to sit out the elections, according to polling.

In a recent development, that’s what happened in another snap election called by Sánchez in 2023. That year, despite losing the popular vote to the center-right People’s Party (PP), Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) managed to remain in power through skillful coalition-building with separatist parties from Catalonia.

Industry observers note that the statistics behind Spain’s housing crisis are eye-popping. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices rose by 80 percent, while rents climbed 87 percent. Nominal wages, by contrast, increased by just 30 percent. An estimated 40 percent of Spanish renters spend an average of 40 percent of their after-tax income on rent and utilities. The burden is even heavier for young people and lower-income households. According to the Bank of Spain, the country currently faces a housing deficit of approximately 750,000 homes, a structural supply gap that could exceed 1 million homes by 2028.

Industry observers note that spain’s housing crisis has its roots in the 2008 financial collapse, when the burst of a speculative property bubble made the country an epicenter of a global crisis that also engulfed the United States. That year, Spain experienced the steepest decline in construction activity of any EU country, and upcoming building virtually ground to a halt. Banks also tightened mortgage lending. The resulting financial crisis, which lasted from 2008 to 2013, brought down thousands of businesses—particularly banks—and pushed unemployment to 25 percent. In 2012, a $124 billion EU-backed rescue package restructured and recapitalized Spain’s financial system.

Efforts to revive the economy had the unintended consequence of exacerbating the housing crisis. One example is the residence-by-investment program, known as the golden visa. Introduced in 2013, the program sought to attract overseas investment by relaxing restrictions on foreign purchases of Spanish property. It granted Spanish residency to anyone acquiring real estate valued at a minimum of $550,000, or depositing $1.1 million in a Spanish bank.

Foreign property purchases surged, fueled by Chinese and Russian investors. But much of the investment flowed into areas where housing was already scarce and expensive: the urban centers of Barcelona and Madrid; the coastal areas of Andalusia, Catalonia, and Valencia; and the Balearic and Canary Islands. In these markets, an influx of foreign capital contributed to rising property prices, putting homeownership increasingly out of reach for locals. Responding to public pressure, the Sánchez government abolished the program last year.

In a recent development, spain’s efforts to promote tourism have also been a mixed blessing. In 2024, the country welcomed a record 94 million international visitors, making it the world’s second-most-visited destination after France. Tourism now contributes $220 billion to the Spanish economy, accounting for 12.6 percent of GDP. But in many cities, the tourism boom has transformed entire neighborhoods into overcrowded tourist zones that overwhelm and alienate locals.

It has been revealed that tourism has also increased demand for foreign workers. According to the Elcano Royal Institute, Spain’s immigrant population stands at 9 million, with approximately 600,000 people arriving annually since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many newcomers compete for low-rent apartments that have traditionally been available to young people and longtime residents. Elcano data also highlights that young Spaniards leave their parental homes and begin to establish independent households at an average age of 30.3, four years later than the EU average. More than 80 percent of Spaniards aged 16 to 29 still live with their parents, compared with an EU average of 68 percent.

Recent findings suggest that for several years, the housing crisis has been convulsing Spanish politics, making the country home to Europe’s most vocal anti-tourism movement. In Barcelona, activists have even sprayed tourists with water guns. City officials have responded with sweeping measures to curb tourism, including some of Europe’s highest tourist taxes, a moratorium on new hotel construction, and a ban on Airbnb-style short-term rentals scheduled to take effect in 2028. But efforts to rein in tourism have set regional and local governments against federal officials in Madrid, who continue to promote tourism expansion by increasing capacity at Spanish airports.

Recent findings suggest that it was an unexpected human tragedy, however, that propelled the housing crisis to the top of Sánchez’s agenda—and helped set the stage for next week’s election. On Sept. 23, police evicted ​Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old disabled woman, from the Madrid apartment she had called home for 70 years. Urbagestión, the investment organization that purchased her building in 2018 from a real estate firm, had sought to raise her rent by 230 percent. When she refused to leave, authorities removed her on a stretcher. Her eviction sparked a wave of protests that culminated in hundreds of housing activists occupying Madrid’s central square. Maricarmen died on Oct. 7.

According to recent reports, shortly after her eviction, the Congress of Deputies rejected a PSOE-backed bill that would have introduced rent caps and restrictions on corporate property purchases. The legislation faced stiff opposition from conservative parties, including Junts, a Catalan separatist party that nominally supports Sánchez. Opponents argued that the proposed restrictions would further constrain housing supply. Earlier this month, responding to popular pressure, Spain’s interim parliament passed a separate housing bill aimed at limiting evictions and curbing real estate speculation. The PP opposed the legislation and pledged to repeal it if elected.

It has been revealed that confident that he will soon be in power, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo welcomed Sánchez’s call for early elections. Polls show a statistical dead heat between the PSOE and the PP. But because neither party is expected to win enough seats to control the Congress of Deputies outright, the far-right Vox—currently Spain’s third-largest party—could emerge as kingmaker. A PP-Vox coalition appears to be a likely outcome of the post-election negotiations. This partnership is not novel: It has been in place at the regional level since 2022 in four autonomous communities: Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, and Andalusia. Vox has used regional governments to advance a nationalist and socially conservative agenda.

Sources indicate that yet the PP might be walking into a trap of its own making. As in 2023, a snap election is giving Sánchez another opportunity to demonstrate his mastery of the political comeback. Polls that year also predicted a potential governing majority for the PP and Vox, but that outcome failed to materialize. Sánchez ultimately outmaneuvered Feijóo by assembling a governing coalition.

It has been revealed that there is a powerful political paradox here: Sánchez is politically vulnerable because of the housing crisis. After all, it was under his watch that housing evolved from a growing concern into a full-blown crisis for Spanish voters. But the opposition’s resistance to his proposed remedies may allow him to turn a political liability into a potentially powerful campaign issue.

Recent findings suggest that framing the election as a referendum on who can best address Spain’s housing woes may offer Sánchez his strongest path to reelection. Rather unexpectedly, the housing crisis has allowed him to shift the campaign’s focus away from corruption and immigration and toward an problem with the potential to mobilize young voters, renters, the elderly, and lower-income households, while also resonating deeply with his Socialist base.

Omar G. Encarnación is the Charles Flint Kellogg professor of politics at Bard College. He is the author of several books, including Spanish Politics: Democracy after Dictatorship, Democracy Without Justice in Spain: The Politics of Forgetting, and, most recently, Framing Equality: The Politics of Gay Marriage Wars.

#134026. Latest Update: Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)

Latest Update: Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side.
  • The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide said on Tuesday.
  • Sources indicate that but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reps. Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide said on Tuesday. The bill, which passed the Senate on Nov. 19 in a 62-33 vote, has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and a wide range of industry groups that are generally GOP allies. Adoption of the rule, typically a party-line affair, would almost certainly lead to final passage and Trump's signature.

Sources indicate that but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in a Nov. 20 letter to colleagues, implored them to come back to work next month to finish out the lame-duck session, citing the permitting bill vote among other things. But it remains to be seen whether defeated lawmakers will take him up on that.

And several Republicans, led by House Freedom Caucus members, have used their leverage in rule votes to extract last-minute changes to legislation from leadership.

Last December, the House considered a bill to overhaul the National Environmental Policy Act from Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman, R-Ark. Ahead of the vote on that rule, Republicans including Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., sought last-minute changes to portions of the bill they were concerned would allow offshore wind projects in the Atlantic Ocean to move forward. Westerman agreed, which in turn caused the American Clean Power Association to withdraw support for the bill.

Harris hasn’t commented yet on the Senate-passed permitting measure. Nor has Freedom Caucus Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, who has called for permitting generally to be a lame-duck priority but was another one of the holdouts on Westerman’s bill last year. Still, the Freedom Caucus is generally on board with permitting legislation and specifically cited it as a priority for the session's waning days.

Republicans are generally expected to support the bill, which enjoys backing from industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, National Mining Association and Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities. The bill’s supporters go beyond the energy sector, including groups like the American Road and Transportation Builders Association and National Association of Home Builders.

And two Democrats — Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, both members of the Blue Dog Coalition — have taken the rare step of crossing the aisle to support Republican rules this year in order to move legislation they support. Both have issued statements that speak favorably of the permitting bill.

Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, one of the bill's lead authors, was enthusiastic about the bill's chances in the other chamber.

"I think there’s a real will there," the West Virginia Republican stated Tuesday after presiding over a pro forma session. "We’ve got to get enough Republicans there to vote, and I think that’s what the speaker is hoping to do. I think he wants to do it under a rule, it sounds like, but I’m very excited about it because I think it’s very, very doable.".

With the path through the House yet to be fully illuminated, a vote under suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds of members present and voting to pass, remains an option. But that's a trickier path given the split among Democrats.

The Senate-passed bill emerged from that chamber in a weaker position than advocates anticipated earlier this month, when 73 senators backed advancing it on an initial procedural vote.

After opponents got through with the measure — including an amendments blockade by Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden that left backers unable to incorporate changes necessary to shore up support — there were just 62 "yes" votes, although there were four absent GOP supporters.

Just 15 out of 47 Democratic caucus members voted for it, including only one member of the Environment and Public Works panel — Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, who wrote the bill with his GOP and Democratic counterparts on EPW and Energy and Natural Resources.

According to recent reports, if there is full attendance on both sides, the threshold for passage on suspension would be about 290 votes. Permitting bill supporters would need about one-third of House Democrats to vote in favor — 71 with current vacancies — similar to their level of Senate Democratic support, assuming all Republicans were on board.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t seem out of the question given that the leadership of the 112-member-strong New Democrat Coalition has expressed support led by the current chair, Brad Schneider of Illinois; the incoming chair, fellow Illinoisan Nikki Budzinski; and Scott Peters, D-Calif., chair of the coalition’s Environment, Climate and Clean Energy Working Group. So has the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.

Recent findings suggest that clean energy groups like the Solar Energy Industries Association and American Clean Power Association back the bill, as do key labor unions including the AFL-CIO, Laborers’ International Union of North America and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL-CIO sent a legislative alert on the bill, which indicates it may include the measure on its annual legislative scorecard.

Sources indicate that but Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is a firm “no” on the current bill. He offered a series of changes on Monday needed to win his support — which have negligible chance of acceptance by the bill’s authors or by Trump, who last week mentioned the bill would put money “back in the pockets of hardworking Americans” and lead to “tremendous amounts of new building.”.

It has been revealed that huffman wants to roll back proposed limits on Endangered Species Act reviews as well as the bill's 150-day limit on judicial challenges and “project certainty” protections intended to bar future administrations from revoking approved permits. Huffman noted the certainty protection would legislate “a third term for Trump” by preventing future administrations from revoking permits for projects that could have detrimental environmental impacts, such as fossil fuel or mining projects.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the official position of the nearly 100-member Congressional Progressive Caucus is opposed. And the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition mentioned it couldn’t support the Senate bill without changes, arguing the measure “includes environmental rollbacks that are concerning to us.”.

Recent findings suggest that two influential Democrats on energy and climate concerns came out against the measure in its current form this week — Reps. Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin of California, who are among the SEEC’s vice chairs. Casten and Levin have worked together on legislation intended to overhaul the transmission permitting system and address energy affordability.

In a statement Casten mentioned the bill would make it “impossible” for a future administration “to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent,” adding he would vote "no" on the Senate-passed bill “with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”.

Casten, who co-founded a clean energy startup before coming to Congress, is currently challenging House Financial Services ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the gavel next year, in a bid resting in part on his environmental bona fides, including sustainable investment and climate-risk regulation.

Levin, an environmental lawyer by trade, praised the bill’s provisions making it easier to build interstate transmission lines, a key bottleneck barring the development of more wind and solar power generation.

In a recent development, “These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon,” Levin noted in his statement. But he said it wasn’t worth the potential environmental costs, adding that “taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”.

Major environmental advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have long been opposed to the measure, as have Native American tribes and representative organizations like the National Congress of American Indians.

Another factor affecting the debate in the House is how to handle a bipartisan package of Senate changes agreed to on both sides of the aisle, but blocked on the floor by Merkley, a staunch opponent of the bill.

That amendment included language making it more difficult to circumvent National Historic Preservation Act rules; giving landowners and state regulators more time to resolve disputes before eminent domain is invoked for transmission projects; and closing loopholes in the bill’s language aimed at making data center developers pay for their own electric-grid upgrades.

It has been revealed that if that amendment had been included, the Senate vote count may have been higher. But attaching it in the House would send it back to the Senate for another round of votes, which may not be practical given the dwindling legislative session. An alternative would be to tuck the amendment into another must-pass bill, like government funding legislation or the National Defense Authorization Act.

The Upcoming Democrat Coalition’s statement, while overall supportive, said the group “will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns.”.

Senate Indian Affairs Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and ranking member Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, worked on changes in the amendment to address concerns tribes and Native American organizations raised about the NHPA section.

It has been revealed that “I'm not going to abandon it just because the bill has been passed now. So working it on the House side, looking for other opportunities to advance it yet this Congress,” Murkowski stated Nov. 20. “So we're not done.”.

Capito told reporters Tuesday that the permitting bill's fate has been invading her dreams.

Sources indicate that "My husband Charlie wakes me up, I’m like in sleep going ‘huh, huh, huh.’ He goes, ‘What’s wrong? What’s wrong?’ I stated, ‘I’m just dreaming about permitting reform,'" Capito recalled. "That’s kind of a sad state of affairs. It was our 50th anniversary.”.

Lauren Green, Jackie Wang and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
